questions.question: A 9-year-old boy presents with a 7-month history of excessive worry regarding his academic performance and his parents' health. He reports being easily fatigued and having difficulty concentrating in class. According to the DSM-5-TR, how many symptoms from the associated list are required to meet the diagnostic criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) in this pediatric case?

answerOptions.text: Only one symptom.
answerOptions.rationale: For children, only one item from the symptom list (e.g., fatigue, irritability, muscle tension) is required to meet Criterion C for GAD, whereas adults require three or more (DSM p. 251; Dulcan p. 312).

answerOptions.text: At least three symptoms.
answerOptions.rationale: While adults require three or more symptoms, the DSM-5-TR makes a developmental allowance for children to meet criteria with only one associated symptom (DSM p. 251).

answerOptions.text: At least six symptoms.
answerOptions.rationale: This exceeds the requirement for both children and adults; Criterion C only lists six total possible symptoms to choose from (DSM p. 251).

answerOptions.text: The number of symptoms is not defined for pediatric populations.
answerOptions.rationale: The DSM-5-TR specifically notes that only one item is required in children, clearly defining the threshold for this population (DSM p. 251).

questions.hint: Check the specific 'Note' under Criterion C for GAD in the DSM-5-TR or Dulcan's text.

questions.question: In the neurobiological model of anxiety described in StahlNeuro, which circuit is primarily associated with the symptom of 'worry,' including apprehensive expectations and catastrophic thinking?

answerOptions.text: Amygdala-centered circuit.
answerOptions.rationale: The amygdala-centered circuit is primarily associated with fear, panic, and phobias, rather than the cognitive symptoms of worry (StahlNeuro p. 366).

answerOptions.text: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop.
answerOptions.rationale: The CSTC 'worry loop,' specifically involving the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), is the hypothetical substrate for worry and ruminations (StahlNeuro p. 367).

answerOptions.text: Mesolimbic dopamine pathway.
answerOptions.rationale: This pathway is more closely linked to reward and the positive symptoms of psychosis, such as hallucinations, rather than anxiety-driven worry (StahlNeuro p. 113).

answerOptions.text: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis.
answerOptions.rationale: While the HPA axis is involved in the endocrine stress response, it is not the specific circuit identified for the cognitive experience of worry (StahlNeuro p. 367).

questions.hint: Consider the 'loop' originating and ending in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).

questions.question: An adolescent girl is being treated for Generalized Anxiety Disorder. According to StahlKids, what is a critical pharmacokinetic consideration when comparing younger children to adults for SSRI dosing?

answerOptions.text: Younger children have slower hepatic metabolism, requiring much lower doses.
answerOptions.rationale: In fact, younger children often have faster hepatic and renal metabolism, not slower (StahlKids p. 139).

answerOptions.text: Younger children may require adult-like doses due to faster hepatic and renal clearance.
answerOptions.rationale: Despite their smaller size, children have proportionately larger livers and faster metabolism, which may necessitate adult-like doses to maintain therapeutic levels (StahlKids p. 139).

answerOptions.text: Renal excretion is immature in adolescents, making them highly sensitive to toxicity.
answerOptions.rationale: Hepatic and renal functions develop early, and drug disposition is often more efficient in children than in adults (StahlKids p. 139).

answerOptions.text: Dosing should always be based strictly on mg/kg without exception.
answerOptions.rationale: While weight is a factor, developmental changes in metabolism (fast hepatic clearance) mean that mg/kg dosing alone may result in subtherapeutic levels in children (StahlKids p. 139).

questions.hint: Focus on the relative size and efficiency of the liver (כבד) in pediatric patients.

questions.question: A clinician is evaluating a 14-year-old for GAD and is considering laboratory testing. According to Dulcan's Textbook, what is the reported yield of universal TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) screening in pediatric patients hospitalized with mood or anxiety disorders?

answerOptions.text: Approximately $25\%$ show clinical thyroid disease.
answerOptions.rationale: This significantly overestimates the prevalence; clinical thyroid disease is actually found in fewer than $1\%$ of these patients (Dulcan p. 330).

answerOptions.text: Fewer than $1\%$ show actual thyroid disease.
answerOptions.rationale: Universal screening has a low yield; thyroid disease is present in fewer than $1\%$ of hospitalized pediatric psychiatric cases, suggesting targeted screening is more effective (Dulcan p. 330).

answerOptions.text: $10\%$ of cases are linked to hyperthyroidism.
answerOptions.rationale: While hyperthyroidism can mimic GAD, its actual prevalence in this population is very low, making universal screening inefficient (Dulcan p. 330).

answerOptions.text: The yield is high only in male children before puberty.
answerOptions.rationale: There is no evidence that prepubertal males have a higher yield; in fact, clinical suspicion based on weight changes or medication history is the best predictor of yield (Dulcan p. 330).

questions.hint: Think about the utility of universal vs. targeted screening for endocrine mimics.

questions.question: When initiating an SSRI in a child with GAD, what is the expected incidence of 'behavioral activation' (אקטיבציה) compared to that seen in adolescents, according to StahlKids?

answerOptions.text: The incidence is approximately the same across all ages.
answerOptions.rationale: Children are specifically noted to have a higher risk of behavioral side effects compared to older groups (StahlKids p. 139).

answerOptions.text: Two- to threefold higher incidence in children than in adolescents.
answerOptions.rationale: Children are more sensitive to these effects, showing a 2-3 times higher rate of behavioral activation and vomiting than adolescents (StahlKids p. 139).

answerOptions.text: Tenfold higher incidence in adolescents due to hormonal changes.
answerOptions.rationale: It is the younger children, not adolescents, who exhibit the significantly higher incidence of activation (StahlKids p. 139).

answerOptions.text: Activation is only seen when SSRIs are combined with SNRIs.
answerOptions.rationale: Behavioral activation is a known side effect of SSRI monotherapy, and its risk is inherently higher in the younger pediatric population (StahlKids p. 139).

questions.hint: Younger children tend to be more sensitive to specific adverse effects than adolescents.

questions.question: A 15-year-old patient with GAD is not responding to initial therapy. The clinician considers adding an $\alpha_{2}\delta$ ligand. According to StahlNeuro, what is the mechanism of action for medications like Pregabalin in treating worry?

answerOptions.text: Blocking postsynaptic $D_{2}$ receptors in the striatum.
answerOptions.rationale: This is the mechanism of antipsychotics, not $\alpha_{2}\delta$ ligands (StahlNeuro p. 113).

answerOptions.text: Binding to the $\alpha_{2}\delta$ subunit of presynaptic voltage-sensitive calcium channels (VSCCs).
answerOptions.rationale: By binding to the $\alpha_{2}\delta$ subunit of VSCCs, these ligands block the excessive release of glutamate in both the amygdala (fear) and CSTC worry loops (StahlNeuro p. 366).

answerOptions.text: Irreversible inhibition of Monoamine Oxidase (MAO).
answerOptions.rationale: This describes the action of MAOIs, which are distinct from the calcium channel modulation seen with Pregabalin (StahlNeuro p. 366).

answerOptions.text: Agonism of postsynaptic $5HT_{1A}$ receptors.
answerOptions.rationale: While $5HT_{1A}$ agonism (like Buspirone) is used in GAD, it is not the mechanism of the $\alpha_{2}\delta$ ligands (StahlNeuro p. 367).

questions.hint: The mechanism involves modulating excitatory neurotransmitter release by acting on calcium channels.

questions.question: Regarding the epidemiology of pediatric anxiety disorders, Dulcan identifies a 'pediatric anxiety triad.' Which three disorders comprise this triad?

answerOptions.text: OCD, PTSD, and GAD.
answerOptions.rationale: While these are all anxiety-related, OCD and PTSD are now classified in different chapters in DSM-5 (Dulcan p. 312; DSM p. v).

answerOptions.text: GAD, Social Anxiety Disorder, and Separation Anxiety Disorder.
answerOptions.rationale: These three disorders frequently co-occur and are referred to as the pediatric anxiety triad (Dulcan p. 312).

answerOptions.text: Panic Disorder, Agoraphobia, and Specific Phobia.
answerOptions.rationale: These are distinct anxiety disorders but do not constitute the primary triad identified for pediatric onset (Dulcan p. 312).

answerOptions.text: Separation Anxiety, Selective Mutism, and ADHD.
answerOptions.rationale: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder, not part of the anxiety triad (Dulcan p. 312).

questions.hint: These three disorders often overlap in presentation and treatment response in children.

questions.question: A clinician uses the GAD-7 scale to monitor an adolescent's response to treatment. According to Dulcan's text, which cut-off score on the GAD-7 is most sensitive and specific for detecting 'severe' anxiety in adolescents?

answerOptions.text: A score of 5.
answerOptions.rationale: A score of 5 usually represents mild anxiety, not severe (Dulcan p. 329).

answerOptions.text: A score of 11.
answerOptions.rationale: A score of 11 is the optimal cut-off for detecting 'moderate' anxiety, while higher scores are needed for severe cases (Dulcan p. 329).

answerOptions.text: A score of 17 or greater.
answerOptions.rationale: Research indicates that a GAD-7 score of 17 or higher reliably detects severe clinical anxiety in adolescents (Dulcan p. 329).

answerOptions.text: A score of 25.
answerOptions.rationale: The maximum score on the GAD-7 is 21; therefore, a score of 25 is impossible (Dulcan p. 329).

questions.hint: Moderate anxiety is detected at 11; severe anxiety requires a significantly higher threshold.

questions.question: According to the Child/Adolescent Anxiety Multimodal Study (CAMS) findings cited in Dulcan, how does the treatment response of SSRIs compare to SNRIs in pediatric anxiety?

answerOptions.text: SNRIs produce faster and more robust improvement.
answerOptions.rationale: The opposite is true; SSRIs are noted for faster and more significant symptomatic reduction (Dulcan p. 331).

answerOptions.text: SSRIs produce faster and greater improvement, with trajectories diverging by week 4.
answerOptions.rationale: SSRIs show a clear advantage in speed and magnitude of effect, and by week 8, SNRIs only achieve $40\%$ of the response seen with SSRIs (Dulcan p. 331).

answerOptions.text: Neither class separates from placebo in pediatric GAD.
answerOptions.rationale: Both classes have demonstrated efficacy compared to placebo, although their trajectories differ (Dulcan p. 331).

answerOptions.text: SNRIs are preferred first-line due to lower rates of activation.
answerOptions.rationale: SSRIs remain first-line despite higher activation rates because they are generally more effective and produce more rapid improvement (Dulcan p. 331; StahlKids p. 756).

questions.hint: Consider the 'divergence' of improvement curves around the one-month mark.

questions.question: How does GAD differ from 'nonpathological' (normal) anxiety in everyday life, as defined in the DSM-5-TR?

answerOptions.text: Normal worries are more likely to be accompanied by physical symptoms like restlessness.
answerOptions.rationale: Physical symptoms are a hallmark of GAD (pathological anxiety), whereas everyday worries typically occur without them (DSM p. 251).

answerOptions.text: Pathological worries are more pervasive, pronounced, and have a longer duration.
answerOptions.rationale: GAD worries are excessive, interfere with functioning, and are more likely to occur without clear precipitants compared to normal life stressors (DSM p. 251).

answerOptions.text: The focus of worry in GAD is strictly limited to one domain, such as finances.
answerOptions.rationale: GAD is characterized by 'generalized' worry over multiple domains, and the focus of worry often shifts over time (DSM p. 251).

answerOptions.text: Normal anxiety is persistent for at least 6 months, whereas GAD is transient.
answerOptions.rationale: By definition, GAD must be persistent (typically $\ge 6$ months), while normal anxiety is often transient and stress-induced (DSM p. 251).

questions.hint: Think about the pervasiveness and the impact on psychosocial functioning.
